summary: This local-news feature examines how shrinking budgets are straining high school sports in the community as the 2023 school year begins. It uses examples from several schools: aging equipment, fundraising by teams, a talented athlete held back, and scholarship-dependent students. It argues that cuts undermine education, community spirit and long-term opportunity, and ends by asking whether the community will step up.
one_line: Budget cuts are straining local high school sports through aging equipment, constant fundraising and lost scholarship chances, prompting calls for community action.
key_facts: The new school year began after September 1, 2023, with local high school sports facing budget cuts to equipment budgets and coaching staff.
On September 15, the Harrington High Hawks kicked off their season with a win.
Coach Mike Jefferson has led the Harrington High Hawks for over a decade and said the team has used the same pads and helmets for several years, far beyond their recommended lifecycle.
Thompson High School's girls' volleyball team has held bake sales and car washes to maintain its competitive edge.
On September 22, team captain Christie Turner said, "It's like we're selling cookies to keep our dreams alive."
On October 5, Adeline Perez of Johnson High, who is aggressively scouted by colleges for track, was reported to have flagging times without a proper training regimen and equipment.
Jason Schmidt of Midtown High is cited as a student for whom an athletic scholarship is the sole financial avenue to college.
The article says athletics teach teamwork, discipline and perseverance, and that funding cuts risk undermining these lessons.
On October 19, Lincoln Heights held its district's annual "Friday Night Lights" football clash.
Rita Gonzales, a local business owner and parent, said, "If we cut back on sports, we're cutting the heart out of our town."

Greg Hall, Athletic Director at Valley Stream High, said, "We're beyond the point of stop-gap solutions" and called on schools, businesses and local governments to build a sustainable future for the programs.
School boards have prioritized academics, and fundraising has shifted from supplementing luxuries to covering basic necessities.
